query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a surface silicide coating (specifically Si-20Cr-20Fe) onto a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) substrate will significantly enhance high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming a protective, self-healing silica-rich oxide scale that limits oxygen diffusion, compared to the uncoated alloy which suffers from rapid oxidation and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with a body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution structure, such as MoNbTaTiW or WVTaTiCr, which exhibits poor oxidation resistance at elevated temperatures due to the formation of volatile oxides and spallation of the oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Application of a Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating via a fused slurry method to the surface of the RHEA substrate.
generation.conditions: Exposure to an oxidizing atmosphere (air) at high temperatures (≥1000 °C) for extended durations (e.g., 50–100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a double-layer silicide structure (outer MSi2, inner M5Si3) that evolves into a continuous, adherent SiO2-rich oxide layer during oxidation, acting as a diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: The silicon in the coating diffuses to the surface during oxidation to form a dense, thermodynamically stable SiO2 layer. This layer exhibits low oxygen permeability and prevents the volatilization of refractory metal oxides (like MoO3 or WO3) that typically cause rapid degradation in uncoated RHEAs. The Cr content aids in forming a protective Cr2O3 layer if SiO2 is compromised, while the coating's structure moves inward, maintaining thickness and integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated RHEA will exhibit a significantly lower mass gain (e.g., <10 mg/cm² after 50 hours) and a parabolic oxidation rate constant compared to the uncoated RHEA, which is expected to show severe spallation and high mass gain (e.g., >100 mg/cm²) due to the formation of non-protective, volatile oxides.
generation.baseline: Uncoated MoNbTaTiW or WVTaTiCr RHEA exposed to the same high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies specifically to RHEAs with BCC structures containing refractory elements (Mo, W, Ta, Nb) susceptible to volatile oxide formation, and assumes the coating remains intact without delamination during thermal cycling.
generation.uncertainty: While the silicide coating strategy is supported by evidence for MoNbTaTiW, the specific long-term stability of the coating-substrate interface under extreme thermal cycling (e.g., >1000 hours) or in the presence of specific impurities (e.g., sulfur) is not fully characterized in the provided evidence. Additionally, the exact diffusion kinetics of Si in different RHEA matrices may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) MoNbTaTiW RHEA with a Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating applied via fused slurry, and (2) uncoated MoNbTaTiW RHEA. Expose both sets to dry air at 1100 °C for 100 hours. Perform cyclic oxidation tests (10 cycles of 10 hours each) to simulate thermal shock.
measurements: Gravimetric mass gain per unit area (mg/cm²) at 24-hour intervals.

Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) of the cross-section to analyze oxide layer thickness, morphology, and elemental distribution (specifically Si and O profiles).
X-ray Diffraction (XRD) to identify oxide phases formed (e.g., SiO2, Cr2O3, MoO3, WO3).
Adhesion testing (scratch test or tape test) to evaluate spallation resistance.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the coated samples exhibit a mass gain greater than 50 mg/cm² after 50 hours, show significant spallation of the oxide layer (loss of >20% of the coating), or if XRD analysis reveals the dominance of volatile oxides (MoO3, WO3) over protective SiO2/Cr2O3 phases, indicating the coating failed to form a protective barrier.

The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature.
